title: Expectation
intro: The expectation is the probability-weighted average of a random variable: the centre of mass of its distribution. Its most powerful property is linearity, which holds with no assumption about dependence.

blocks.caption: Defined when the sum or integral converges absolutely.

blocks.text: The expectation exists only when $E\vert X\vert < \infty$. Some perfectly good random variables have no mean: the Cauchy distribution, or the payout of the St Petersburg game (double the stake until the first head), whose expectation is $\sum2^k2^{-k} = \infty$. Averages of samples from such variables never settle (The Law of Large Numbers (#/probability/limit-theorems/law-of-large-numbers)).
The law of the unconscious statistician
You do not need the distribution of $g(X)$ to find its mean; weight $g$ by the distribution of $X$. The name is a joke about how naturally people use it without noticing it needs proof.

blocks.tex: E[aX + bY + c] = a\,E[X] + b\,E[Y] + c
blocks.caption: True for any random variables with finite means, dependent or not.

blocks.text: Combined with indicators, linearity solves problems whose distributions are hopeless. To count something, write the count as a sum of indicators and add their probabilities. The number of fixed points of a random permutation of $n$ items is $\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{\text{item } i \text{ stays put}\}$, each with probability $1/n$, so its mean is exactly 1 for every $n$, although its distribution needs inclusion–exclusion.

Expectation is not multiplicative in general: $E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]$ holds for independent variables, not for all. Nor does it commute with nonlinear functions: $E[g(X)]\ne g(E[X])$ in general, and Jensen's inequality says which way the gap goes for convex $g$ (Inequalities (#/probability/toolkit/inequalities)).
Each unit of $X$ is counted once by the event that $X$ reaches it. This often avoids computing the PMF at all; for the geometric distribution it gives $\sum(1-p)^{k-1} = 1/p$ at once.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
# Linearity: the expected number of fixed points of a random permutation is 1 for every n
for n in (5, 50, 500):
    fp = [np.sum(rng.permutation(n) == np.arange(n)) for _ in range(20000)]
    print(f"n = {n:3d}: mean number of fixed points = {np.mean(fp):.3f}")
# Geometric: trials until the first success has mean 1/p
p = 0.2
print(f"geometric, p = {p}: simulated mean {rng.geometric(p, 200000).mean():.3f}, 1/p = {1/p}")
# The tail-sum formula E[X] = sum P(X >= k) for X in {1, 2, ...}
k = np.arange(1, 400)
print("sum of P(X >= k) =", round(np.sum((1 - p) ** (k - 1)), 6))
# St Petersburg: a finite simulation of a variable with infinite mean never settles
pay = 2.0 ** rng.geometric(0.5, 10 ** 6)
for N in (10 ** 2, 10 ** 4, 10 ** 6):
    print(f"St Petersburg mean of first {N:>7} plays: {pay[:N].mean():.2f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: the mean number of fixed points is 1.002, 0.992 and 1.009 for $n = 5$, 50 and 500. The geometric mean with $p = 0.2$ is 4.993 against $1/p = 5$, and the tail sum gives exactly 5. The St Petersburg running mean reads 20.4, 13.7 and 33.1 after $10^2$, $10^4$ and $10^6$ plays: it never settles, because there is no mean to settle on.

blocks.title: Mean of a reciprocal
blocks.text: $X$ is 1 or 2 with probability 1/2 each. Compare $E[1/X]$ with $1/E[X]$.
solution: Not equal: $1/x$ is convex on $x > 0$, so Jensen gives $E[1/X]\ge1/E[X]$.

blocks.title: Empty boxes
blocks.text: Throw $n$ balls independently and uniformly into $n$ boxes. What is the expected number of empty boxes? Evaluate for $n = 10$.
solution: Box $i$ is empty with probability $(1 - 1/n)^n$; by linearity the mean number empty is $n(1 - 1/n)^n$.

blocks.title: Coupon collector
blocks.text: How many rolls of a fair die are needed, on average, to see all six faces?
solution: After $k$ distinct faces, each roll is new with probability $(6-k)/6$, so the wait is geometric with mean $6/(6-k)$.
